item.title: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
item.description:
Fleeing violence and persecution, Rohingya refugees walk after crossing the Naf River from Myanmar into Bangladesh on Oct. 9, 2017. Photo by Fred Dufour/AFP via Getty Images In a 9-6 vote, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in the northern Rakhine State. This is a remarkable moment for the Rohingya people and international justice – the first time, in fact, that the ICJ has ever ruled that a state committed this crime. It is a historic victory, worthy of celebration in a world where good things happen all too sparsely. Especially because it is a victory won against a global legal architecture almost designed to never find that a state committed genocide. item.title: Rohingya genocide survivor: ‘perpetrators will have to face consequences’
item.description:
Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."

item.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches one light-day milestone
item.description:
This illustration shows Voyager 1 passing by the rings of Saturn. NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space . During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then traveled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium : the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating. But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. item.title: California Bans Waymo From Freeways. Is That Really Safer?
item.description:
Waymo's driverless cars are no longer on California's freeways, at least for now. On November 11, the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) issued an order immediately barring Waymo vehicles from rides or testing on California highways, though they can continue operating on other streets. On Tuesday, the order was made public, and the DMV confirmed that it had banned the cars from California freeways. A DMV spokesperson said Waymo's operation poses an "imminent hazard to public safety," citing "recurring incursions" by the company's vehicles into active construction zones, according to KQED News. The DMV pointed to two specific instances in the last week. One involved three Waymos entering an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101, putting workers at risk. item.title: Welcome to Software Beirut
item.description:
Last week, when it briefly looked like the world was collapsing while I sat on the tarmac, I wrote about the arrival of Software Beirut —“where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.” I’m no Tom Friedman , but many people seemed to enjoy the phrase and encouraged me to keep using it even as outages at the FAA, Chase, and Microsoft proved to be isolated incidents unrelated to bad guys using advanced AI. Well, hold my mustache wax! Because I’m doubling down. The fact that all of the software chaos appears to have had boring causes doesn’t negate my point—it improves it. Software Beirut is not an event but an environment, shaped by three forces that arrived at roughly the same time: AI is exposing vulnerabilities in critical software at unprecedented speed; the rush to fix the bugs creates its own hair ball…
